previous_admission_summary.summary_paragraph: A 68-year-old male with a history of non-ischemic cardiomyopathy, atrial fibrillation, restrictive lung disease, type 2 diabetes, and recently treated lung cancer was admitted for a three-day history of worsening shortness of breath and orthopnea. Initial evaluation showed pulmonary edema on chest X-ray, elevated BNP, and mild renal impairment. His symptoms improved with diuresis, steroids, azithromycin, nebulizer treatments, and CPAP. Amiodarone was discontinued due to possible pulmonary toxicity. He was in sinus rhythm, and his INR rose to 3.1, prompting warfarin hold instructions. He was discharged home with improved respiratory status, continuing a short course of prednisone and azithromycin, new nicotine patch for smoking cessation, and home CPAP setup. Follow-up was arranged with pulmonology, oncology, and primary care.

FINDINGS: 

Fiducial marker and known left mid lung opacity laterally is better seen on
prior CT scan and known pulmonary nodules are not clearly delineated on this
portable exam. Increased interstitial markings throughout the lungs are again
noted but are likely chronic. Increased bibasilar opacities are likely
atelectasis given the low lung volumes. The cardiomediastinal silhouette is
stable. Left chest wall single lead pacing device is again seen.

IMPRESSION: 

No definite acute cardiopulmonary process. Known pulmonary nodules are better
seen on prior CT scan.

INDICATION:  72 with nonlocaliziing ab pain and tenderness history of AAA
repair.

TECHNIQUE:  MDCT images were obtained from the lung bases to the pubic
symphysis without the administration of intravenous contrast.  Axial images
were interpreted in conjunction with coronal and sagittal reformats.

DLP:  941 mGy-cm

COMPARISON:  CT abdomen and pelvis ___ and ___. CTA
chest ___.

FINDINGS: 

There are stable right lower lobe pulmonary nodule measuring 8 and 6 mm
(2:8;2:3).  Partially calcified pleural plaque is unchanged (02:14). There is
bibasilar atelectasis. An AICD is incompletely imaged. No pericardial
effusion.

ABDOMEN:

The examination is limited secondary to the lack of intravenous contrast.
Within this limitation, the non-contrast enhanced appearance of the liver is
unremarkable. There is cholelithiasis without evidence of cholecystitis
(02:25). There is fatty atrophy of the pancreas. The spleen, adrenal glands,
and kidneys are unremarkable.  No renal calculi are identified.

The stomach, small bowel, and large bowel are unremarkable in appearance
without dilation or wall thickening. The appendix is not visualized but no
inflammatory changes seen in the right lower quadrant.  There is no
retroperitoneal or mesenteric lymphadenopathy by CT size criteria. There is no
free abdominal fluid or pneumoperitoneum.

There is atherosclerotic disease of the abdominal aorta branching into the
iliac arteries. There is no abdominal aortic aneurysm.  There is evidence of
infrarenal abdominal aortic aneurysm repair. There is no retroperitoneal
hematoma.


PELVIS:

The bladder is well distended and normal in appearance. There is no pelvic
side-wall or inguinal lymphadenopathy by CT size criteria. No free pelvic
fluid is identified.

OSSEOUS STRUCTURES: Multilevel, multifactorial degenerative changes are seen
throughout the visualized thoracolumbar spine. No focal lytic or sclerotic
lesion concerning for malignancy.
